claims.text: Rapid Joule heating of nanoparticle-loaded carbon supports produces highly defective turbostratic graphite with abundant edge sites.
Nanoparticles partially intercalate and bond at defective edge sites of turbostratic graphite, producing strong anchoring.
Defect-rich turbostratic graphite provides numerous nanoparticle nucleation sites and increases nanoparticle–support binding energy.
Strong support anchoring limits nanoparticle mobility and suppresses agglomeration during high-temperature operation.
Carbon-supported nanoparticles stabilized by this mechanism remain thermally stable through 1173 K.
Defect-mediated anchoring will remain effective during thermoelectric operation approaching 1923 K.
Suppressing nanoparticle migration and agglomeration preserves a near-equiatomic, single-phase CrMnFeCoNiCu solid solution.
The initial material consists of equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu nanoparticles on carbon supports.
Controlled pretreatments can produce carbon supports with tunable defect densities and highly defective turbostratic-graphite regions.
A low-defect inert-carbon control can isolate the effect of support defect density.
External support stabilization competes with intrinsic alloy diffusion and alloy thermodynamics.
High-defect supports will retain smaller and more uniformly dispersed nanoparticles than low-defect supports after thermal cycling.
High-defect supports will better retain near-equiatomic composition and a single-phase state than low-defect supports after thermal cycling.
Minimal anchoring on low-defect carbon facilitates nanoparticle migration and agglomeration.
Nanoparticles on low-defect carbon undergo compositional drift over time.
The proposed mechanism applies to carbon supports processed to contain turbostratic graphite.
Applicability to supports other than turbostratic carbon, alloys other than CrMnFeCoNiCu, and prolonged operation near 1923 K is unestablished.
At temperatures approaching 1923 K, intrinsic alloy diffusion may overcome substrate-induced stabilization.
TEM, XRD, XPS, and elemental mapping can compare particle size, dispersion, phase identity, and compositional homogeneity between high- and low-defect supports.

Failure of the high-defect support to produce a statistically significant improvement in structural integrity, dispersion, and compositional uniformity relative to the low-defect control would falsify the anchoring hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and predicted outcome broadly assert preservation during operation up to 1923 K, whereas the boundary and uncertainty fields state that effectiveness near 1923 K is unestablished and may be overcome by intrinsic diffusion.
